lessons.title: Trace plan, customer subscription and schedule state
lessons.overview: Subscription engineering starts by keeping three concepts separate: the plan definition, the individual customer's subscription lifecycle, and generated or scheduled work. The service owns these records and their validated transitions. An administrator changing a plan is not the same operation as changing an existing customer's state, and a schedule calculation is not permission to invent pricing, rollover, pause, cancellation or payout rules.

steps.label: Identify the object
steps.detail: Determine whether the requirement changes a plan, a customer subscription or schedule/execution state.

steps.label: Trace the caller
steps.detail: Follow customer versus administrator routes and the Craves JWT/role or ownership check.

steps.label: Trace lifecycle rules
steps.detail: Locate service validation for current state, requested transition and relevant schedule constraints.

steps.label: Trace persistence
steps.detail: Identify subscription_schema records and which values must remain historical.

steps.label: Trace downstream work
steps.detail: Separate persisted lifecycle state from later order/schedule/notification actions and their independent evidence.

lessons.example: An administrator can update an approved plan definition without that operation itself proving every existing subscriber has been migrated to the new terms.
lessons.lab: Trace one customer subscription operation and one plan/schedule operation from route to service and persistence. Mark every point where an approved commercial policy is required.
lessons.pitfall: Do not treat a technical schedule field as an implicit answer to an unresolved cancellation, rollover or billing rule.

questions.prompt: What should an engineer identify first in a subscription change?
options: The owning object: plan, customer subscription or schedule
questions.explanation: Clear aggregate ownership prevents plan and customer-state changes from being conflated.

questions.prompt: Does schedule code define commercial policy by itself?
questions.explanation: Implementation follows approved policy; it does not create it.

lessons.title: Implement an approved lifecycle or schedule feature
lessons.overview: Once a subscription rule is approved, convert it into an explicit state and scheduling contract. Define the trigger, allowed source states, resulting state, effective time, idempotency behavior and customer-visible outcome. Implement the rule in the service/schedule layer, persist durable facts, use migrations for schema changes, and keep downstream order or notification creation recoverable. Avoid embedding policy constants in multiple controllers or clients.

steps.label: Record the approved rule
steps.detail: Reference the authorized business decision and translate it into precise technical inputs and outputs.

steps.label: Define state/time semantics
steps.detail: Specify allowed states, effective timestamps, timezone assumptions and retry behavior.

steps.label: Implement centrally
steps.detail: Place lifecycle/schedule rules in the owning service instead of duplicating them in web and mobile clients.

steps.label: Persist durable evidence
steps.detail: Store the state/time facts needed to explain what happened after configuration or plan data changes.

steps.label: Integrate idempotently
steps.detail: Ensure scheduled downstream work cannot create duplicate orders or messages when a job retries.

steps.label: Expose through contracts
steps.detail: Update admin/customer DTOs and UI only with approved state and explanatory data.

lessons.example: For an approved pause behavior, the technical design states exactly when pause becomes effective and how repeated requests behave; it does not guess how unused meals or money should be handled.
lessons.lab: Take a fictional already-approved lifecycle rule and create its state table, effective-time rules, persistence fields, retry key, API changes and tests. Explicitly list commercial questions that would still require Product/Finance input.
lessons.pitfall: Hard-coding an unapproved commercial assumption makes future correction a customer-impacting migration instead of a policy configuration change.

questions.prompt: Where should shared subscription lifecycle logic live?
questions.explanation: Centralized service logic gives all clients one authoritative lifecycle contract.

questions.prompt: What must repeated scheduled execution avoid?
questions.explanation: Schedulers are routinely retried and therefore require idempotent downstream work.

lessons.title: Test time, retries and policy-safe rollback
lessons.overview: Subscription bugs often hide in time boundaries and repeated scheduler runs. Tests should cover lifecycle transition validity, ownership, clock/timezone boundaries, duplicate scheduling, missed/replayed jobs and downstream failures. Release evidence must prove the approved rule is configured as intended. Recovery should restore execution without silently rewriting historical customer state or applying a newly invented financial rule.

steps.label: Freeze time in tests
steps.detail: Use controlled timestamps to test boundary behavior rather than relying on the machine clock.

steps.label: Test invalid transitions
steps.detail: Verify state changes are rejected when the current lifecycle state does not permit them.

steps.label: Replay the scheduler
steps.detail: Run the same due work more than once and assert one downstream business effect.

steps.label: Simulate downstream failure
steps.detail: Ensure a failed order/notification action can be retried without changing the subscription decision incorrectly.

steps.label: Verify production policy
steps.detail: Compare configured behavior with the approved rule before customer-facing activation.

steps.label: Recover historically
steps.detail: Preserve audit/lifecycle evidence and use an approved correction path when customer state already changed.

lessons.example: If a scheduler ran twice, recovery should deduplicate the generated work and preserve the single intended lifecycle outcome rather than changing the customer's plan to hide the duplicate.
lessons.lab: Build a time-based test matrix around a fictional approved renewal/pause boundary using a fixed clock, duplicate scheduler execution and one downstream failure. Do not define real pricing or refunds.
lessons.pitfall: Changing production subscription state to make a test pass destroys the evidence needed to understand the original failure.

questions.prompt: Why use a fixed clock in subscription tests?
questions.explanation: Deterministic time makes schedule/lifecycle boundary tests reliable.

questions.prompt: What should recovery preserve after a lifecycle bug?
questions.explanation: Historical evidence is necessary for safe correction and auditability.
